PROTOCOL
Evidence map of nutrient interventions 
for major depression: a systematic review 
protocol
Dongbo Zhang1,2†, Chenqi Li1,3†, Xue Tian4†, Gen Miao1, Wenjing Shi1, Hongtao Lu1, Yicui Qu1, Mengyu Cai1, 
Yuxiao Tang1*, Hui Shen1* and Biao Gao5*
Abstract
Background Depression severely impacts quality of life globally. While traditional treatments show efficacy, many 
patients respond poorly. Nutritional interventions demonstrate potential as safe, economical adjunctive therapies. 
However, current evidence is scattered and heterogeneous, lacking systematic evaluation. This study aims to systematically evaluate evidence for various nutritional interventions in depression and create an evidence gap map (EGM).
Methods We will conduct a systematic review using the EGM approach. Major medical databases will be searched 
for relevant studies published up to present. Two independent researchers will screen literature, extract data, 
and assess evidence quality. Multiple tools will be used for quality assessment: Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool 2.0 for RCTs, 
ROBINS-I for non-RCTs, Newcastle–Ottawa Scale for observational studies. The GRADE system will be employed 
for overall evidence grading. EPPI-Reviewer Web will generate the EGM. We will analyze evidence distribution, time 
trends, and explore impacts of population characteristics and depression subtypes.
Discussion This study will provide critical methodological references for nutritional psychiatry. Expected results 
include identifying nutrient categories with robust antidepressant evidence, evaluating evidence distribution 
for different interventions, and exploring differential effects across populations and depression subtypes. Findings 
will inform individualized nutritional strategies, improve clinical guidelines, and potentially influence public health 
policies.
Systematic review registration CRD42024590644. Date of registration: 30/09/2024.
Keywords Depression, Nutrition, Evidence gap map, Systematic review

Innovative points
These innovative points specifically pertain to the integration of nutrition and psychiatry.
1. Methodological innovation: This study represents the 
first application of evidence gap mapping (EGM) in 
nutritional psychiatry, specifically to systematically 
evaluate nutritional interventions in depression. This 
method can identify areas with sufficient and insufficient evidence, providing a basis for future research 
directions and clinical decision-making.
2. Multidimensional evidence integration and quality

assessment: The study comprehensively covers various nutrients (such as vitamins, minerals, lipids, and 
amino acids) and employs multiple quality assessment tools (Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool 2.0, ROBINS-I, Newcastle-Ottawa Scale) for different study 
designs, with GRADE for overall evidence grading.
3. Interdisciplinary integration and clinical translation: 
By combining nutrition science with psychiatry, this 
study provides a scientific foundation for developing individualized nutritional intervention strategies 
and improving clinical guidelines, promoting the 
development of nutritional psychiatry as an emerging 
interdisciplinary field.
4. Dynamic evidence assessment mechanism: Using 
EPPI-Reviewer establishes a sustainable and updatable evidence assessment system. This ensures that 
research results can continuously reflect the latest 
developments in the field, providing dynamically 
updated evidence support for long-term policy formulation and clinical practice.
5. Public health policy impact: The research results provide a scientific basis for developing nutrition-based 
strategies for the prevention and management, with 
the potential to drive innovation in relevant public 
health policies (Fig. 1).

Introduction
Depression is a major global public health issue that 
severely impacts patients’ quality of life and social functioning [1]. Despite advances in pharmacological treatments, a considerable proportion of patients still respond 
poorly to existing therapies [2], especially those with 
treatment-resistant depression (TRD). Consequently, 
exploring new intervention measures has become an 
urgent issue to address. In recent years, nutritional interventions have shown great potential as safe, economical, and feasible adjunctive therapies in the treatment of 
depression. Research indicates that nutritional factors are 
closely related to the onset, development, and prognosis 
of depression [3]. As a safe, economical, and accessible 
adjunctive therapy, nutritional interventions demonstrate 
significant potential for application in the management of 
depression [4, 5].
As an emerging interdisciplinary field, nutritional psychiatry aims to study the interactions between nutrition 
and mental health, providing a theoretical foundation 
for nutritional interventions in mental disorders. Scholars have conducted numerous interventional studies on 
various nutrients, including omega-3 polyunsaturated 
fatty acids, vitamin D, B vitamins, zinc, and magnesium. 
These nutrients have been found to have positive effects 
on alleviating depressive symptoms, improving cognitive 
function, and enhancing quality of life in different studies [6–10]. However, the results of existing research are 
often scattered and highly heterogeneous, with varying

quality of evidence for results after using different nutrients, and a comprehensive systematic evaluation of the 
evidence in this field is lacking. This limits the formulation of clinical decisions and the efficient utilization of 
research resources.
Evidence gap maps (EGMs) are emerging tools for 
evidence integration and visualization, presenting the 
distribution characteristics of evidence between interventions and outcome indicators in a specific field 
through a matrix format [11]. While Campisi SC et  al. 
[12] demonstrated an EGM’s utility by examining micronutrients’ impact on youth depression, these methodological instruments have broader applications in 
identifying research gaps, prioritizing future studies, and 
informing policy development [13–15].
This systematic review aims to evaluate and visually 
present the effectiveness of various nutritional interventions for depression, examining the impact of nutrients 
(such as vitamins, minerals, fatty acids, and amino acids) 
on symptoms, biochemical markers, imaging results, 
incidence, remission, relapse rates, and quality of life, 
compared to placebo, standard care, or non-nutritional 
interventions. By assessing different ages, genders, and 
depression subtypes, we will identify areas with sufficient 
and insufficient evidence, quantify the quality and quantity of findings, and reveal research gaps. The synthesis 
will provide valuable insights for future research, clinical 
practice, public health policies, and the development of 
nutritional psychiatry, offering strategies for managing 
depression.
Overview
A complete flowchart of the evidence gap map (EGM) 
protocol for nutrient interventions in depression is presented in Fig. 2.
The data acquisition process follows the PRISMA 
guidelines [16] as illustrated in Fig. 3.
Inclusion and exclusion criteria
We will adopt the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) framework to construct the inclusion and exclusion criteria for our systematic review 
[17], supplemented by additional parameters including 
study design, publication date, language, and geographical scope. This approach not only adds structural clarity 
to the literature screening process but also significantly

enhances the scientific rigor and methodological precision by adhering to this established methodological 
framework.
Inclusion criteria
Population
• Include: Studies involving patients diagnosed with 
depression (including mild, moderate, severe depression; first-episode and recurrent depression) based 
on structured or clinical interviews (e.g., DSMIV/V, ICD-10 criteria) or validated rating scales (e.g., 
Hamilton Depression Rating Scale [HAMD], Beck 
Depression Inventory [BDI]).
• Exclude: Animal studies (e.g., livestock, pets, fisheries), in vitro experimental studies, and subjects who 
are at high risk of depression but have not yet been 
formally diagnosed. Studies with participants having multiple mental health disorders will be included 
only if the depression-related outcomes are reported 
separately.
Intervention
• Include: Supplementation of individual nutrients 
or clearly defined combinations, including vitamins 
(e.g., A, C, D, E, B-group vitamins), minerals (e.g., 
zinc, magnesium, iron, calcium, selenium), fatty 
Zhang et al. Systematic Reviews (2025) 14:124 Page 4 of 12
acids (e.g., omega-3, omega-6), amino acids (e.g., 
tryptophan, S-adenosylmethionine).
• Exclude: Dietary patterns, whole-food interventions without clear specification of nutrients, complex nutrient combinations without individual 
nutrient effect clarification, rare nutrients with 
limited generalizability (e.g., chromium, molybdenum, vanadium). Studies exclusively proposing 
theoretical mechanisms or correlations without 
actual intervention outcomes. Purely theoretical or 
biochemical studies focused on neurotransmitters, 
immune, or biochemical markers without direct 
clinical evaluation of depressive symptoms. Studies 
primarily investigating adverse effects of nutrient 
interventions for depression without clear beneficial intervention results.
Comparator
• Include: Studies using placebo, standard/routine 
care, or other non-nutritional interventions as 
comparators.
Outcome
• Include: Studies reporting changes in depressive 
symptoms measured by validated scales (HAMD, 
BDI, Montgomery-Asberg Depression Rating Scale

[MADRS]), remission or relapse rates, incidence of 
depression, quality of life outcomes, or biochemical 
markers relevant to depression.
• Exclude: Studies not explicitly reporting outcomes 
related to depressive symptoms, or focusing solely 
on non-primary depressive symptoms (e.g., sleep 
disturbances, fatigue) without separate depression 
symptom assessment. Studies where outcomes of

depression are entirely attributed to medical or 
substance-use-related factors without independent 
evaluation of primary depressive symptoms.
Study types
• Include: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs), cohort 
studies, case-control studies, cross-over design studies, case reports.
• Exclude: qualitative studies, letters, editorials, 
opinions, conference abstracts, retracted literature, 
duplicate publications, book chapters (unless also 
published as peer-reviewed journal articles), and 
study protocols. Ongoing or incomplete studies, 
studies with no available results or conclusions. 
Letters or editorial communications without substantial data, errata, or corrections without substantive content. Book literature unless simultaneously published as a peer-reviewed journal article.
Language
Fig. 3 PRISMA flow diagram for data acquisition. Legend: This PRISMA flow diagram illustrates the systematic literature identification, screening, 
and selection process for the review of nutrition interventions in depression. The diagram is divided into four main stages: identification records

database is to be specified. Screening: this stage involves removing duplicates and screening records based on abstracts. Exclusion criteria at this 
stage include non-English, non-journal, lacking essential information, retracted literature, non-human subjects, duplicate publications, and in vitro 
experiments. Eligibility: full-text articles are assessed for eligibility. Exclusion criteria at this stage include undiagnosed subjects, dietary interventions,

the focus on relevant studies of single-nutrient interventions for clinically diagnosed depression. Specific exclusion criteria at each stage help 
to maintain the focus on high-quality, relevant studies that can inform evidence-based practices in nutritional psychiatry. Including snowball papers 
thoroughly captures relevant literature that might not have been identified through the initial database searches

• Include: Studies published in English.
• Exclude: Non-English literature.
Date
• Include: No date limits.
• Geographic limits.

Search strategy
Databases: PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of 
Science.
Search period: No time restrictions; covering all available records from database inception.
Main Search Terms: Including “depression,” “major 
depressive disorder,” “nutrient,” “vitamin,” “zinc,” “magnesium,” “selenium,” “lithium,” “iron,” “copper,” “mineral elements,” “mineral supplements,” “micronutrients,” “trace 
elements,” “amino acids,” “fatty acids,” “lipids,” “phospholipids,” “triglycerides,” “fatty acid*,” “lipid*,” “phospholipid*,” “triglycerid*,” “omega-3,” “omega-6,” etc.
Search strategy example (PubMed):
#1 ((((((((((((((((((((vitamin A) OR (vitamin E)) OR 
(vitamin D)) OR (vitamin K)) OR (vitamin K1)) OR (vitamin K2)) OR (vitamin k3)) OR (vitamin K4)) OR (vitamin 
B1)) OR (vitamin B2)) OR (vitamin B3)) OR (vitamin PP)) 
OR (vitamin B5)) OR (vitamin B6)) OR (vitamin B12)) 
OR (vitamin B9)) OR (vitamin M)) OR (vitamin B7)) OR 
(vitamin H)) OR (vitamin C)) OR (vitamin).
#2 depression.
#3 #1 AND #2
The actual search strategy will be adjusted according to

the characteristics of different databases and nutrients. 
The search strategy will combine subject terms and free 
terms, adjusted according to the characteristics of different databases and nutrients.
Gray literature and manual searches: In addition to 
the primary database searches, we will perform targeted 
Google searches and systematically visit the websites of 
relevant organizations and charities—such as the Mental 
Health Foundation, Mind UK, Food for the Brain Foundation, Food and Behaviour Research, the American 
Society for Nutrition, Think Through Nutrition, and The 
Centre for Nutritional Psychology—to identify any grey 
literature (reports, theses, or other non-indexed studies).
Clinical Trial Registries: We will query clinical trial registries, including ClinicalTrials.gov and WHO ICTRP, to 
capture unpublished studies.
Forward citation chasing: For all studies meeting the 
inclusion criteria, citation indexes such as Web of Science 
and Scopus will be used to identify subsequent studies 
that have cited these key articles.
Supplementary search strategy: We will review the reference lists of all relevant systematic reviews identified 
during the scoping and screening process. This step is 
intended to ensure that any eligible primary studies cited 
in these reviews are not overlooked.
Condensed post-search bias assessment: Following 
study selection, publication bias will be evaluated using 
funnel plots, Egger’s test (if ≥10 studies are included), 
and time-trend analysis. Outcome reporting bias will be 
examined by comparing published outcomes with preregistered data, and sensitivity analyses will be conducted 
to assess the impact of unpublished studies. The overall 
influence of bias on evidence quality will be appraised 
using the GRADE criteria[18].
Literature screening and data extraction
The screening process follows the PRISMA (Preferred 
Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines[16] and utilizes the literature management tool NoteExpress for efficient management. After 
deduplication, two independent reviewers will conduct 
the screening process in two stages:
Title/abstract screening
Reviewers will independently screen titles and abstracts 
using the comprehensive, pre-defined inclusion and 
exclusion criteria. To ensure consistency and clarity 
in applying these criteria, a calibration exercise will be

conducted at the outset of the screening. This exercise 
is intended to standardize reviewer interpretation and, 
if necessary, refine the criteria. Any disagreements that 
arise during this stage will be resolved through discussion, and if consensus cannot be reached, a third reviewer 
will serve as an arbitrator.
Full‑text screening
For studies that pass the initial screening, a full-text 
review will be performed by the same two independent 
reviewers. Prior to commencing full-text screening, a 
separate calibration exercise will be conducted to ensure 
that the inclusion/exclusion criteria are interpreted and 
applied consistently at this more detailed level. Disagreements during full-text screening will be addressed 
through direct discussion, with a third reviewer being 
consulted if needed.
Data extraction
Following the full-text screening, data from the included 
studies will be extracted independently by two reviewers using a pre-designed extraction form. A calibration 
exercise on a subset of studies will be performed before 
Zhang et al. Systematic Reviews (2025) 14:124 Page 7 of 12
full-scale data extraction to ensure that the extraction 
process is clear and uniformly applied. Any discrepancies 
or ambiguities identified during this calibration will lead 
to revisions in the extraction form or criteria as necessary. Specific extracted content includes:
• Basic study information: Study title, first author, 
publication year, study location, sample size, study 
design, etc.
• Participant characteristics: Age, sex, diagnostic criteria, disease duration, etc.
• Interventions: Detailed recording of specific measures for the intervention and control groups (such as 
the types of nutrients used, dosage, duration of the 
intervention).
• Outcome indicators: Changes in the severity of 
depression symptoms (such as scores using HAMD, 
BDI), incidence, remission rate, relapse rate of 
depression, quality of life, etc.
• Study results: Including effect size, 95% confidence 
interval, and main study conclusions.
• Evidence quality assessment: Assess the quality of 
evidence through the GRADE system [18] and record 
potential sources of bias.
Coding and data management
Coding Process: Coding will be done simultaneously

with data extraction. Literature lacking essential elements will be excluded. Newly discovered literature 
that meets the inclusion criteria will be incorporated 
in a timely manner.
Missing Data: Attempts will be made to contact the 
original authors for important missing data. If it is 
not obtained, the potential impact will be explained 
and discussed in the analysis.
Additional Sources: Supplementary literature discovered during data extraction and analysis will be 
added to ensure completeness of the data.
Quality and risk of bias assessment
Given that this study is an evidence mapping exercise, we 
will employ quality assessment tools appropriate for various study designs, while focusing on the unique aspects 
of nutritional interventions in depression management:
For RCTs: We will utilize the Cochrane Risk of Bias 
Tool 2.0 (RoB 2) [19], emphasizing:
a. Randomization process
b. Allocation concealment
c. Blinding of intervention implementation
d. Completeness of outcome data
e. Bias in outcome measurement
f. Selective reporting
Notably, for nutritional intervention studies, we will 
pay additional attention to the assessment and reporting 
of intervention adherence.
For observational studies (Cohort and Case–Control 
Studies), the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS)[20] will be 
employed, with appropriate adjustments for nutritional 
intervention research characteristics, such as:
a. In the “Exposure assessment” section, special attention is given to the reliability of nutritional intake 
assessment methods.
b. In the “Outcome assessment” section, consideration 
is given to the appropriateness of depression assessment tools.
c. Designs that do not align with the NOS (or are more 
complex in confounding factors) will be evaluated 
using the ROBINS-I tool[21].
For cross-sectional studies, an adapted version of the 
NOS [22] will be used, incorporating specific assessments 
of nutritional status evaluation methods and depression 
diagnostic criteria.
For case series studies, the NIH Quality Assessment 
Tool [23] will be applied, focusing on study objectives, 
sample selection, intervention description, outcome 
measurement, follow-up duration, and statistical analysis.
Two researchers independently conduct quality and

risk of bias assessments at both study and outcome levels, using pre-designed forms. This dual-level approach 
allows us to consider overall study quality and specific 
biases affecting individual outcomes. Disagreements will 
be resolved through discussion or third-party arbitration. 
The assessment process will adhere to the guidelines of 
each tool to ensure objectivity and consistency. We will 
provide detailed quality assessment reports for each 
study, including scores for each assessment domain and 
an overall evaluation. These results will be used to interpret study reliability, inform the GRADE assessment of 
evidence quality [18], guide sensitivity analyses, and provide context for interpreting our findings in the EGM. 
This approach will enable a nuanced understanding of 
the quality and reliability of evidence for nutritional 
interventions in depression.
OCEBM and GRADE systems
Following the aforementioned quality assessments, 
we will employ a comprehensive approach utilizing 
both the Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine (OCEBM) Levels of Evidence and the Grading of 
Zhang et al. Systematic Reviews (2025) 14:124 Page 8 of 12
Recommendations, Assessment, Development and 
Evaluations (GRADE) system to evaluate the overall 
quality of evidence. The OCEBM Levels of Evidence 
emphasize hierarchical classification of different types 
of research evidence [24], while the GRADE system 
offers a more holistic assessment methodology. GRADE 
not only considers the quality of individual studies but 
also evaluates the consistency, directness, and precision of the overall body of evidence, as well as publication bias [18, 25]. This integrated approach allows us to 
synthesize the quality assessment results from various 
study designs discussed in the previous section, forming a comprehensive judgment on the overall quality 
of evidence. Such a thorough evaluation is particularly 
crucial for evidence mapping studies, providing a 
robust foundation for our findings and conclusions.
Main tools
EPPI‑reviewer web
EPPI-Reviewer Web (version 4.14.0.0) is a specialized 
tool for systematic reviews and evidence gap maps 
(EGM) developed and maintained by the Social Science 
Research Unit at University College London (UCL)

[26]. This tool supports systematic literature screening, 
data extraction, and complex multivariate analysis, and 
generates intuitive evidence visualization maps through 
its interactive interface.
• Rationale for Use: It has the capability to support 
large-scale data management, efficiently handle 
thousands of pieces of literature, and support synchronous operations of multiple users in team collaboration. At the same time, it can display the distribution of evidence in matrix form and generate 
interactive bubble charts based on evidence quality 
and quantity, providing great convenience for evidence synthesis and analysis of the study.
• Advantages: Its powerful literature management 
and screening functions can help researchers 
organize and process large amounts of literature 
data efficiently. It supports multi-user collaboration, structured data extraction, and flexible literature screening based on researcher-defined criteria. In addition, it has built-in PRISMA function 
modules, ensuring the transparency and scientific 
nature of the literature search and screening process.
• Limitations: It requires a high level of complexity in 
data processing, which requires researchers to have a 
certain technical background and data management 
capability. Generating large-scale maps may consume 
considerable computational resources.
Other tools
• NoteExpress: Used for the management of literature, helping to efficiently organize and process the 
retrieved literature. After deduplication and classification, data will be imported into EPPI-Reviewer for 
further analysis.
• GitHub: The generated EGM map will be stored in a 
GitHub repository, allowing researchers or readers to 
access the interactive online map by clicking the link. 
This makes the EGM not only a static literature summary tool but also a dynamic display of time changes 
in different evidence and intervention effects, facilitating real-time screening of relevant evidence by 
clinicians and policymakers according to different 
needs.
Data synthesis and analysis
Following the Cochrane Handbook and the PRISMA 
statement [16], we will assess the heterogeneity of the 
included studies and synthesize the data using quantitative or qualitative methods. Given the nature of our EGM 
approach, traditional meta-analytic techniques such as

effect size calculation (e.g., risk ratios, mean differences) 
or statistical pooling methods (e.g., fixed-effect or random-effects models) may not be applicable. Instead, we 
will focus on categorizing and summarizing the evidence 
based on the type of nutrient intervention, study design, 
population characteristics, and reported outcomes. The 
quantity of evidence will be represented by the number 
of studies in each category, while the quality of evidence 
will be assessed using the GRADE approach. Where 
possible, we will report the direction and magnitude of 
effects descriptively, noting any trends or patterns across 
studies.
To synthesize the data, we will construct a matrix-style 
evidence map, with rows representing nutrient interventions (various nutrient subcategories) and columns representing outcome indicators (including biochemical, 
scoring, and descriptive aspects of depression). Each cell 
will be filled with the quantity and quality of evidence. 
Using an interactive EGM tool, we will visually present 
the distribution and gaps in evidence for different nutrients across depression outcomes, providing a comprehensive overview of the current evidence landscape for 
nutritional interventions in depression.
A descriptive analysis will systematically summarize 
the characteristics of the evidence distribution, including the total volume of evidence for each nutrient-outcome combination, study design patterns, and trends in 
reported effects. Using the GRADE approach to assess 
evidence quality, we will qualitatively assess the strength 
Zhang et al. Systematic Reviews (2025) 14:124 Page 9 of 12
of the antidepressant effects of nutrients, addressing 
both the presence and the strength and reliability of the 
evidence.
Where necessary, subgroup analyses will explore differences across specific populations (e.g., age, gender, 
depression subtypes) or types of nutrient interventions. 
Sensitivity analyses may be conducted to evaluate the 
impact of including or excluding studies based on quality 
or other factors.
This comprehensive approach will offer a clear picture 
of the evidence landscape for nutritional interventions 
in depression, highlighting both known areas and key 
research gaps.
Subgroup analysis plan (potential)
Nutrient type subgroups: Vitamins (e.g., A, C, D, E, B

group); minerals (e.g., zinc, magnesium, iron, calcium, 
selenium); fatty acids (e.g., omega-3, omega-6); amino 
acids (e.g., tryptophan, S-adenosylmethionine).
Population subgroups: Age groups (e.g., children, adolescents, adults, elderly); gender; special populations 
(e.g., pregnant women, patients with chronic diseases).
Depression type subgroups: Mild, moderate, severe 
depression; first-episode and recurrent depression.
Study design subgroups: RCTs; cohort studies; case–
control studies; cross-over design studies.
Intervention characteristic subgroups: Duration of 
intervention (short-term, medium-term, long-term); 
dose of nutrients (low, medium, high dose).
Analysis methods:
• Create separate views on the evidence map for each 
subgroup, showing the evidence distribution within 
that subgroup.
• Use the EPPI-Reviewer Web tool to generate interactive charts that show the quantity and quality of evidence for each subgroup.
• Conduct descriptive analysis, compare differences in 
evidence distribution between subgroups, and identify potential patterns or trends.
• Explore the heterogeneity among different subgroups 
and discuss possible reasons for these differences.
Sensitivity analysis
To assess the robustness of our findings, we will conduct 
the following sensitivity analyses:
Impact of study quality: We will include only highquality studies (based on scores from quality assessment 
tools) and compare their results with the overall findings.
Influence of study design: We will separately analyze results from randomized controlled trials and 
observational studies to evaluate the impact of study 
design on conclusions.
Sample size effect: We will compare results from large 
sample studies (≥ 100 participants) with those from small 
sample studies (< 100 participants).
Publication year influence: We will compare results 
from studies published within the last five years with 
those from earlier studies to assess the impact of temporal factors.
Nutrient type effect: We will conduct separate analyses 
for major nutrient categories (e.g., vitamins, minerals, 
fatty acids) to evaluate the influence of different types of 
nutrients.

Through these key sensitivity analyses, we aim to evaluate the reliability and consistency of our research findings 
while identifying important factors that may influence 
our conclusions. This streamlined approach will enable 
us to focus more effectively on the most critical potential 
influencing factors, while maintaining analytical depth 
and practicality.
Reporting limitations
Evidence heterogeneity and quality imbalance
When building the EGM, there may be significant differences in study design, intervention methods, and 
outcome indicators in different studies. This heterogeneity will affect the complete evaluation of evidence, especially when comparing different study results. Therefore, 
although EGM can systematically display the distribution 
of evidence, it cannot eliminate biases caused by differences in study design.
Lack of quantitative effect estimates
As EGM focuses on displaying evidence distribution 
rather than combining effect sizes, this study cannot provide quantified intervention effects like a meta-analysis. 
Evidence maps can help identify areas where evidence 
is dense or scarce, but EGM cannot draw definitive conclusions about the specific effects of interventions. This 
means that EGM cannot directly compare the efficacy of 
nutrient interventions in different studies.
Impact of low‑quality evidence
Despite efforts to grade research quality, some evidence 
remains of low quality, particularly in fields dominated by 
observational studies. These may influence overall conclusions and judgments regarding certain interventions; 
therefore, more high-quality randomized controlled trials 
are still necessary to verify these findings.
Timeliness of evidence
While Fig.  1 highlights the EGM’s ability to be continuously updated as new evidence emerges, the results 
Zhang et al. Systematic Reviews (2025) 14:124 Page 10 of 12
presented in this study reflect only the literature available up to the search completion date. In other words, 
our current evidence map provides a static snapshot of 
the evidence distribution, and it does not capture future 
studies that may be published after this date. Although 
the EGM methodology inherently supports dynamic 
updates, the present analysis is limited to the existing 
dataset, and its findings cannot represent the evolving 
research status beyond the search period.
Interpretation of research gaps
While EGM can effectively identify research gaps, it

should be noted that evidence gaps do not necessarily mean that an intervention is ineffective; it may just 
be due to insufficient research in the field or lack of 
thorough exploration. Therefore, the “evidence gaps” 
shown on the map should be viewed as opportunities for 
future research, not as a negation of the intervention; it 
may also indicate less interest from researchers in that 
intervention.
Risk of bias in included studies
Although we have extensively searched multiple databases and adopted strict inclusion and exclusion criteria, 
there may still be publication bias (i.e., positive results 
are more likely to be published), especially for small sample or early studies. EGM cannot quantify publication 
bias as meta-analysis does, but descriptive analysis can 
preliminarily identify this problem. This means that the 
results of EGM can overestimate the evidence for certain 
interventions.
Expected results
This study is expected to create an evidence map of nutritional interventions for depression, intuitively reflecting 
the distribution of evidence for intervention effect for different nutrients on various clinical and population indicators of depression. Preliminary speculation suggests 
that there may be significant differences in the quantity 
and quality of evidence among different nutrients. For 
example, omega-3, vitamin D, B vitamins, zinc, and magnesium may have relatively more research supporting 
their antidepressant effects[27–30], but the evidence is 
mainly based on observational studies, with overall low 
quality, urgently needing more prospective cohort studies and large-sample RCTs for verification. At the same 
time, there may currently be a lack of sufficient evidencebased support for the antidepressant effects of common 
nutrients such as vitamin A, vitamin C, and vitamin E. 
EGM is expected to intuitively reveal evidence gaps in 
these areas, pointing the direction for future targeted 
research. Furthermore, from the perspective of intervention effects, it is anticipated that there may be more 
evidence to improve depressive symptoms than to prevent the onset of depression, suggesting that research on 
nutrients in primary prevention of depression should be 
strengthened. For different subgroups of the population, 
the effects of nutritional interventions can vary, with 
potentially stronger research targeting specific groups

such as pregnant women, children, and the elderly. EGM 
will also help to discover current research deficiencies in 
certain types of nutrients and populations.
Discussion
This study systematically maps the evidence landscape 
for nutritional interventions in depression using the evidence gap map (EGM) method, providing an essential 
methodological reference for the emerging field of nutritional psychiatry. The results help identify areas with sufficient and insufficient evidence and offer crucial insights 
into formulating future research priorities and guiding 
clinical decision-making.
Methodological innovation and application
This study represents the first application of EGM in the 
field of nutritional psychiatry, demonstrating the advantages of this tool in the integration and visualization of 
complex and diverse evidence. This method can intuitively present the distribution of evidence for effective 
interventions in depression, revealing research gaps and 
providing guidance for the rational allocation of research 
resources. Future studies could consider extending this 
method to other mental health domains.
Importance of evidence quality assessment
By grading the evidence using the GRADE tool, the study 
emphasizes the importance of high-quality research in 
guiding clinical practice. The results may indicate that 
certain nutritional interventions (such as omega-3, vitamin D) have more high-quality evidence supporting 
them, while other areas may suffer from poor-quality 
research. This finding underscores the immense potential need for more high-quality, large-sample randomized 
controlled trials to validate the effectiveness of nutritional interventions.
Individualized nutrition intervention strategies
The study results may reveal the differential effects of 
various nutrients in specific populations or subtypes 
of depression. This provides a foundation for developing individualized nutritional intervention plans. For 
example, patients with vitamin D deficiency may require 
specific supplementation strategies, folic acid may be 
essential for patients with certain genotypes, and highly 
prevalent in specific populations may be closely related 
to certain nutrient deficiencies. Future research should

further explore the feasibility and effectiveness of this 
individualized approach.
Necessity of interdisciplinary collaboration
The results of this study could further underscore the

importance of collaboration between nutrition and psychiatry. Future research should strengthen this collaboration, exploring the synergistic effects of nutritional 
interventions with traditional treatment methods (such 
as pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy).
Policy impact and public health significance
The results of the study may have important implications for depression prevention and management strategies. For example, there may be a need to emphasize the 
importance and effectiveness of certain vital nutrients 
more in public health policies or to use specific nutritional interventions preventively in high-risk populations.
Research limitations and future directions
This study may have some limitations, such as publication bias and heterogeneity among included studies. 
Future research should consider more detailed subgroup 
analyses, exploring the impact of different demographic 
characteristics and disease subtypes on the effects of 
nutritional interventions. Additionally, more studies are 
needed that focus on long-term effects and safety.
In conclusion, this study provides a comprehensive evidence landscape for nutritional interventions in depression through systematic evidence mapping. This helps 
optimize current clinical practice and points the direction for future research, promoting the development of 
nutritional psychiatry as an emerging discipline. With the 
conduct of more high-quality studies and the accumulation of evidence, nutritional interventions are expected to 
become an indispensable part of comprehensive depression management, ultimately improving patient quality of 
life and overall health.
Dissemination plan
Academic publication
We plan to publish the research results in high-quality journals relevant to the field. We will consider open 
access publication to increase the accessibility of the 
research. The findings will also be presented at international conferences related to nutrition and psychiatry.
Online resources
We will use GitHub to store and share the generated evidence gap map (EGM), allowing other researchers direct 
access to and use the interactive EGM. The research findings will be disseminated through the web channels of 
relevant professional organizations. Within the bounds 
of ethics and privacy, we will share the research results 
and data on academic social media platforms (such as 
ResearchGate or Academia.edu) to facilitate further analysis and validation.
Institutional dissemination and policy impact

We will release research briefs or press releases through 
the official channels of participating institutions (such as 
Naval Medical University). We will consider submitting 
policy briefs to relevant health departments. The research 
results may be used to update or formulate related clinical practice guidelines.
Public dissemination
To ensure findings reach a broader audience, we will also 
develop dissemination materials specifically tailored for 
the general public. These materials will include accessible summaries, infographics, and policy briefs, designed 
to communicate the importance and implications of our 
findings to non-academic audiences and stakeholders.
